papers_processed.extraction_notes: Paper is a 3D U-Net deep-learning segmentation/detection model for intracranial aneurysms on CT angiography (CTA) volumes. This is medical imaging (CT volumes + 3D segmentation), explicitly outside MLGG scope which covers EHR/registry tabular binary classification, not imaging. Reviewer comments confirm modality: '3D UNet-based deep learning framework for the segmentation of intracranial aneurysms in CTA images'. Skipped extraction per OUT_OF_SCOPE_ON_RECHECK guidance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Since the definition of acute kidney injury is a rise in serum Cr of a certain degree, prior levels of Cr and Cr trajectory (and levels/trajectories of things which closely track Cr, such as BUN and Phos) of course contribute to a very high AUC. Rising Cr is not just a predictor (like sepsis), it is 'in the causal pathway' so to speak.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors thanked the reviewer and agreed; they noted the paper had already shown the model performed well when Cr/BUN were explicitly left out, addressing the definition-variable leakage concern.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My concern with this entire literature has to do with the fact that I am not sure what clinicians are supposed to do with this type of information. There are no therapies which have been proven in randomized controlled trial to reduce risk of development of acute kidney injury in high risk patients (even if we were to be given a 24 to 48-hour advanced warning).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors responded with KDIGO-grounded actionable steps (medication review, fluid/hemodynamic optimization, care bundles) and cited evidence that electronic alert care bundles improve AKI outcomes; added a paragraph to Discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: One can quibble with some of the clinical decisions that were made e.g. 'Burn patients were also excluded since serum creatinine becomes a less reliable tool in assessing renal function during hypermetabolic phase.' There are numerous other situations in which Cr performance is also problematic, such as cirrhosis, amputation, or muscle wasting diseases which lead to changes in Cr production.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed but noted burn patients are a small fraction; no further cohort changes made.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The GTM is not compared with any algorithm and I recommend to report results also for logistic regression as baseline. This would help to support some considerations made in text, that are very general but only based on one method. I would be curious to see if the deterioration with LR is proportional or maybe the choice of the model plays a factor in the external performances.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added LASSO logistic regression baseline (page 5 and 9 plus Supplemental Figures 4 and 8). For GBT, AUROC went from 0.81 (temporal) to 0.73 median (external); for LASSO from 0.78 to 0.68 — LASSO consistently worse but with comparable deterioration pattern.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The utility of adjMMD is not clear in my opinion. Experiments show that refitting the model in the external sites work better than just using the pre-trained models. So, what is the point of knowing the deterioration in advance? I would like the author to address better this issue and clarify more the usefulness of adjMMD in practice, highlighting some best practices depending on the score (Should we use the model as it is? Should we consider another model for the new site? Should we re-train? And so on).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded Discussion to articulate adjMMD use-cases by data-maturity tier: low-maturity sites use the imported model with adjMMD-based confidence flag; high-maturity sites use adjMMD to decide on recalibration vs full refit. Added implementation guidance on page 16.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The most novel aspect of this work is the adjMMD and its strong association with decrement in AUC. However, the experiments performed thus far are not convincing regarding its association with the change in AUC. More experiments should be performed, including: 1. Deriving models with each other the other six sites being the derivation site to confirm that this relationship still holds; 2. Testing this association with another commonly used machine learning model (e.g., elastic net); 3. Testing this association with a trimmed list of variables (e.g., age, BMI, vitals, CBC, BMP, and trends) that are likely to be collected at all hospitals.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors ran three additional experiments: (1) each of six sites as derivation site for GBT, (2) same with LASSO, (3) limited-GBT with trimmed common-variable list. Mixed-effects model gave slope 0.257 (95% CI [0.08, 0.44]) confirming positive adjMMD-vs-AUC-drop relationship across sites, models, and feature sets.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Were ICD and CPT codes included in the models? If so, we these codes from prior to the admission or from the current admission? Codes from the current admission are often not available in real-time due to delays in billing filing, so these variables should not be included in the model.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed both ICD and CPT codes were included; ICD codes were from past encounters, CPT codes captured procedures during current stay. They acknowledged that delayed CPT billing means a real-time deployment would need to ingest procedure orders instead, and added this caveat to Limitations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Can you clarify whether patients were censored at 7 days if still in the hospital? If so, did you still test the model in patients with LOS of >7 days or was the model not validated in those patients? This should be added to the limitations, as LOS>7 days is not uncommon, especially in critically ill patients.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed censoring at 7 days and that patients with LOS > 7 days were not tested; added to Limitation and Future Work section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The details about how the data were split into different cohorts for training and validation should be included in the Methods. Additional information regarding how the refitting procedure during the transportability tests are needed. For example, what proportion of the external data was used to refit the model vs. test the model? Did the refitting combining the training cohort with part of the external site's data?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added more details about experimental setup and refitting procedure in the Experimental Design paragraph on page 19.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although the CDM allowed for the inclusion of additional variables, is this really an interpretable model when applied to an individual patient? Could clinicians really understand a model with 30,000 predictor variables, with likely thousands of them combining to form small, but meaningful effects on predictions?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors emphasized white-box GBT exposes top-feature contributions per patient; provided Figure 2 marginal plots and an interactive Shiny dashboard (sxinger.shinyapps.io/AKI_ishap_dashbd) for patient-level explanations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: If the new hospital data are available, why not just refit the data using those data as a matter of practice as opposed to calculating transportability metrics first? Additional discussion regarding this and the advantages of using adjMMD should be discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued not all hospitals have sufficient quality data to refit/build their own model; adjMMD lets data-poor sites assess transportability and data-rich sites decide between recalibration, refit, or full revision. Added a paragraph to Discussion.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Two-round review with 3 reviewers. Round 1 had substantive comments from all three; Round 2 saw R2 fully satisfied and R3 satisfied with one minor citation suggestion (Koyner et al). R1 did not appear in Round 2. PDF structure: reviewer comments first (pages 1-4), then point-by-point author responses (pages 5-11), then Round 2 review and final response (pages 12-14). Notable: R1's comment #4 is essentially praise for the leave-Cr-out robustness test, which is a strength rather than a concern — handled by including it as the C01 'definition variable' concern since it raises a leakage-flavored issue authors had to defend. R1 #1 was praise (white-box approach) and is captured as a strength only.

Paper is a deep-learning platform combining 17 CNNs for DLBCL diagnosis from histopathology whole-slide / 400x H&E photographic images of lymph node biopsies. This is histopathology imaging, explicitly outside MLGG scope (which covers EHR/registry tabular binary classification, not WSI/pathology). Reviewers (R2 hemopathologist, R3 ML methodologist) confirm modality: 'diagnosis of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) from pathologic images'. Skipped extraction per OUT_OF_SCOPE_ON_RECHECK guidance. Of note: R3 raised an interesting potential patient-level leakage concern ('it is possible that a patient has some of his slides in the training set, and some in the test set?') — a textbook MLGG-S01 issue, but on imaging data so out of MLGG's tabular EHR scope.
